answer.rationale:
Two memories are load-bearing here and both deserve a source check. memory_c2 is the one that would justify switching outright: it reports a sharp unit-cost cut and quick onboarding at the low-cost vendor. But it is dated 'last year' and archived on day 38, and I cannot tell from the consolidated line whether that switch happened while the line had slack. Onboarding that was 'quick' with buffer is not evidence that it is quick at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and switching primary supply 14 days before expiry on a line with zero slack is exactly where a migration hiccup converts a cost win into missed committed volume. memory_c4 is the basis for my intended action: benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on both price and terms. I want to confirm how much movement was actually recovered, because that determines whether negotiation can realistically approach the 18% mandate or only part of it.

Intended action: negotiate_terms, using the low-cost vendor's compliant quote as the benchmark. This is the only direction that pursues the cost mandate while holding delivery risk flat, and it is supported by three independent memories (c4 on negotiation yield, c1 on incumbent integration stability across two cycles, c6 on volume pricing). It also preserves the option value of the low-cost quote rather than spending it.

Downstream value risk: the 18% mandate is a hard finance target and negotiation may land short of it. If the incumbent will not move far enough, the honest read is that this cycle buys continuity and partial savings, and the next review should qualify the low-cost vendor as a second source (per memory_c3, which removed a single point of failure and held through a shortage) so a later primary switch can be made from a tested position rather than under expiry pressure. I am also wary of memory_c6's multi-year lock: a long term cuts unit cost but forecloses the switch that may be needed if the mandate persists, so I would push for cost relief on a term short enough to keep that door open. I am not treating any of these inherited lines as settled; if the archive shows c2's switch occurred under materially different capacity conditions, or c4's recovered margin was small, my ranking shifts.
